f:adr: A US-traded security that stands for shares of a foreign company held by a depositary bank.
f:after-hours: Trading before the 9:30 a.m. Eastern US open (pre-market) or after the 4:00 p.m. close (after-hours).
f:analyst-actions: What an analyst does to a rating: upgrade moves it up, downgrade down, reiterate keeps it, initiate starts coverage.
f:average-price-target: The average of the price targets published by the analysts a data provider tracks.
f:backlog: Signed orders or contracts not yet delivered, and so not yet counted as revenue.
f:basis-points: A percentage point (pp) is the plain gap between two percentages; a basis point (bp) is a hundredth of one.
f:bear-market: Conventionally, a fall of 20% or more from a recent high; a correction is a fall of 10% or more.
f:beat-miss: A result above the analysts' consensus estimate is a beat; one below it is a miss.
f:beta: How much a stock has tended to move when the market moves: 1 means in step, above 1 bigger swings.
f:bid-ask-spread: The gap between the highest price a buyer offers (bid) and the lowest a seller accepts (ask).
f:blockchain: A shared record of transactions kept in copies by many independent computers.
f:bond-yield: A bond's yearly return at today's price, which moves opposite to price; the yield curve plots yields by maturity.
f:breakeven-inflation: An ordinary Treasury yield minus the TIPS real yield of the same maturity; markets read it as expected inflation.
f:broker-ratings: Overweight, Outperform, Neutral and other house ratings
Firms' own rating words, which each firm maps to Buy, Hold or Sell; Overweight and Outperform usually mean Buy.
f:bull-bear-case: The argument for a stock doing well (bull) and against it (bear); bulls expect prices to rise, bears to fall.
f:buyback: A company buying its own shares on the market, which cuts the share count.
f:cagr: The steady yearly growth rate that would turn a starting value into an ending value over several years.
f:call-option: The right, not the obligation, to buy something at a set price (the strike) by a set date.
f:callable: A bond or preferred share the issuer can buy back early, at a set price after a set date.
f:cap-rate: A property's yearly net operating income divided by its value or price.
f:capex: Money spent on long-lasting assets such as factories, equipment, networks or data centers.
f:catalyst: A known or expected event that could move the share price, such as an earnings report or court ruling.
f:cet1-ratio: A bank's highest-quality capital as a percentage of its risk-weighted assets; a higher ratio means a thicker loss cushion.
f:combined-ratio: An insurer's claims plus expenses as a percentage of the premiums it earned; under 100% means underwriting made money.
f:company-size: Rough size bands by market cap: large-cap is commonly $10 billion or more, mid-cap about $2 billion to $10 billion.
f:consensus-estimate: The average forecast of the analysts covering a company, for revenue, EPS or another figure.
f:consensus-rating: The average of covering analysts' ratings, expressed as one word on a scale from Strong Sell to Strong Buy.
f:contango: Later futures months priced above nearer ones (contango), usually from holding costs, or below them (backwardation), usually from scarcity.
f:cost-of-carry: Cost of carry and fair value
Holding costs over time, interest and storage less income; a future's fair value is today's price adjusted by that cost.
f:coupon: The fixed yearly interest a bond pays, as a percentage of its face value, usually in two payments a year.
f:credit-rating: A rating agency's grade of a borrower's ability to repay; BBB− and above is investment grade, below it high yield.
f:crypto-supply: Circulating supply, max supply and crypto market cap
The coins issued so far (circulating) and the protocol's hard limit, if any (max): 21 million for bitcoin.
f:cryptocurrency: Digital money recorded on a blockchain, with no bank or government issuing it.
f:currency-hedged: Using contracts to cancel most of the effect of exchange-rate moves on a fund's foreign holdings.
f:current-ratio: Assets that turn into cash within a year divided by bills due within a year: a test of short-term liquidity.
f:cyclical: Tied to the economy (cyclical), or selling what people buy regardless (defensive); a secular trend runs through the cycles.
f:debt-to-equity: Borrowings divided by shareholders' equity; higher means more of the business is financed with debt.
f:depreciation: An expense spreading a long-lived asset's cost over its years of use; amortization does the same for intangibles.
f:dilution: When new shares are issued, for pay, deals or fundraising, each existing share owns a smaller slice of the company.
f:distribution-yield: A fund's cash payouts as a percentage of its price.
f:dividend: Cash a company pays its shareholders out of profits, usually every quarter in the US.
f:dividend-yield: A year's dividends per share as a percentage of the share price.
f:dollar-index: ICE's index of the US dollar against six major currencies, mostly the euro; higher means a stronger dollar.
f:dot-plot: A Fed chart, published four times a year, of officials' views on where the federal funds rate should be.
f:dow: A stock-market average of 30 large US companies, weighted by share price rather than market value.
f:drawdown: A fall from a previous high, in percent; the maximum drawdown is the largest such fall over a period.
f:duration: Roughly the percent a bond's price moves the opposite way per 1 percentage point change in yield; convexity refines it.
f:earnings-call: A company's quarterly results (the earnings release) and the conference call where management answers analysts' questions.
f:ebitda: Operating profit before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization: a rough gauge of cash earnings from operations.
f:efficiency-ratio: A bank's costs as a share of revenue; lower is leaner. Net charge-offs are loans written off, net of recoveries.
f:enterprise-value: The stock-market value plus debt, minus cash: roughly what a buyer would pay for the whole business.
f:eps: A company's profit divided by its number of shares: the profit that belongs to each share.
f:etf: A fund whose shares trade on a stock exchange throughout the day, like a company's shares.
f:ev-ebitda: The value of the whole business, debt included, divided by its yearly operating earnings before depreciation.
f:exchange: The marketplace where a stock is listed and traded, such as the New York Stock Exchange or Nasdaq.
f:expense-ratio: A fund's yearly running costs as a percentage of its assets, taken out of the fund's value rather than billed.
f:ffo-affo: The REIT version of earnings: net income with property depreciation added back and property-sale gains removed.
f:fiscal-year: A company's 12-month accounting year, which need not match the calendar; Q1 to Q4 are its quarters.
f:float: Shares outstanding are all shares issued; the float is the part the public can trade, excluding insiders' and governments' stakes.
f:fomc: The Federal Reserve committee that sets the target range for the federal funds rate, meeting eight times a year.
f:forward-guidance: What a central bank says about the likely path of its policy rate.
f:forward-pe: The share price divided by the earnings per share analysts expect over the coming year.
f:free-cash-flow: The cash a business generated after paying its running costs and its investment in equipment, buildings and the like.
f:futures-contract: An exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell a set amount of something later, at a price fixed today.
f:gaap: The US accounting rules (many companies abroad use IFRS); non-GAAP figures leave out items such as stock-based pay.
f:gic: A Canadian fixed-term deposit at a set rate, usually locked in until maturity; a US certificate of deposit is similar.
f:goc-bond: A loan to Canada's federal government paying fixed interest twice a year; Real Return Bonds are the inflation-linked kind.
f:greeks: Measures of how an option's price responds to the stock's price (delta, gamma), time (theta) and volatility (vega).
f:gross-margin: The share of each sales dollar left after the direct cost of making or buying what was sold.
f:guidance: Management's own forecast for coming results, usually revenue, margins or EPS, given alongside earnings.
f:hyperscaler: One of the few companies that run data centers at vast scale, such as Amazon, Microsoft and Google.
f:impairment: Cutting an asset's book value when it is worth less than recorded; goodwill is the premium paid in acquisitions.
f:implied-volatility: The market's estimate of how much a price will swing, as a yearly percentage, backed out of option prices.
f:index-fund: A fund that copies an index instead of picking stocks, usually by holding its members in the index's proportions.
f:insider: A company's officers, directors and owners of over 10% of its shares, who must report their trades to the SEC.
f:institutional-investors: Organizations that invest large pools of money for others, such as fund managers, pension funds and insurers.
f:ipo: A company's first sale of shares to the public, and the start of trading on an exchange.
f:iron-condor: An options combination that profits if the price ends inside a range, with both the premium and the loss capped.
f:leverage: The use of borrowed money, which magnifies gains and losses for shareholders; net debt is debt minus cash.

f:leverage.futures: Controlling a large position with a small deposit, so gains and losses are large next to the cash put up.

f:ma-200: The average closing price over the last 200 trading days, about ten months.
f:ma-50: The average closing price over the last 50 trading days, about ten weeks.
f:margin-call: A demand to add cash when losses push a margin account, the deposit backing a position, below the required minimum.
f:margin-expansion: A rising share of revenue kept as profit, often from operating leverage: fixed costs make extra sales mostly profit.
f:mark-to-market: Valuing a position at today's market price.

f:mark-to-market.futures: In futures, the daily settlement: each day's gain is paid into the account and each day's loss taken out.

f:market-cap: What the stock market values the whole company at: the share price times the number of shares.

f:market-cap.crypto: A coin's price times its circulating supply: what the market values all the coins issued so far at.

f:market-maker: A firm that quotes prices to buy and sell all day and earns the gap between them, the bid-ask spread.
f:mer: The Canadian measure of a fund's yearly cost: management fee plus operating expenses and taxes, as a percentage of assets.
f:moat: A lasting advantage that keeps competitors from taking a company's profits, like a moat around a castle.
f:money-market-fund: A fund of very short-term, high-quality debt such as T-bills, paying near short-term rates; not a bank deposit.
f:moving-average: The average of the last several closing prices, recalculated each period, which smooths out swings to show the trend.
f:multiple: A price divided by a measure of the business, such as P/E; re-rating means the market pays a different one.
f:nasdaq-100: An index of the 100 largest companies listed on the Nasdaq exchange, leaving out financial companies.
f:nav: Net asset value per share: a fund's assets minus liabilities, divided by its shares, set once a day.
f:net-assets: The total value of everything a fund owns minus what it owes: the size of the fund.
f:net-debt-to-ebitda: How many years of operating earnings it would take to repay debt net of cash.
f:net-interest-margin: A bank's core spread: interest earned minus interest paid, as a share of the assets that earn interest.
f:net-profit-margin: The share of sales that ends up as profit after every cost, interest payment and tax.
f:one-off-items: Gains or charges that won't repeat, such as a legal fine, an asset sale or a write-down.
f:open-interest: The number of futures or options contracts still open at the end of a day.
f:operating-cash-flow: The cash a company's day-to-day business generates in a period.
f:operating-margin: The share of sales left after all running costs, including research, marketing and administration, but before interest and taxes.
f:organic-growth: Growth excluding acquisitions and businesses sold; constant currency also removes exchange-rate effects; same-store sales count only established stores.
f:payout-ratio: The share of profit paid out as dividends.
f:peg-ratio: The P/E divided by the expected yearly earnings growth rate; near 1, the price roughly matches the growth.
f:policy-rate: The short-term interest rate a central bank sets, such as the Fed's federal funds target range.
f:preferred-share: A share that usually pays a fixed dividend and ranks ahead of common shares, but behind lenders.
f:price-target: An analyst's estimate of where the share price will be, usually 12 months out.
f:price-to-book: The share price divided by book value per share: the company's assets minus liabilities, per share.
f:proof-of-stake: A way of adding blocks in which validators lock up the network's coins as a security deposit instead of mining.
f:proof-of-work: Bitcoin's block-adding race: miners solve a computing puzzle to win new coins, a reward that halves about every four years.
f:put-option: The right, not the obligation, to sell something at a set price (the strike) by a set date.
f:rate-base: For a regulated utility, the value of the network on which regulators let it earn a set return.
f:rating-scale: Strong Buy, Buy, Hold, Sell, Strong Sell
Analysts' rating scale: Buy expects a stock to outperform its market or sector, Hold to keep pace, Sell to lag.
f:reit: A company that owns or finances income-producing property and must pay at least 90% of taxable income as dividends.
f:retained-earnings: All the profits a company has kept over its life, after losses and dividends paid; part of shareholders' equity.
f:revenue: The money a company takes in from selling its goods and services, before any costs.
f:revenue-growth: How much more, or less, the company sold than a year earlier, in percent.
f:roe: Profit as a percentage of shareholders' equity (ROE) or of everything the company owns (ROA, return on assets).
f:roic: After-tax operating profit as a percentage of all the money lenders and shareholders have invested in the business.
f:roll: Closing a futures contract near expiry and opening the same position in a later one to keep the exposure.
f:rotce: A bank's profit as a percentage of its tangible common equity: equity minus goodwill, intangibles and preferred stock.
f:rsi: A 0–100 momentum gauge: above 70 is commonly read as overbought, below 30 as oversold.
f:sales-load: A sales charge some mutual funds take when you buy (front-end) or sell (back-end), on top of the yearly fee.
f:same-day-options: Options traded on the day they expire; S&P 500 index options now expire every trading day.
f:sec-filings: The SEC regulates US securities markets; listed companies file annual (10-K), quarterly (10-Q) and major-event (8-K) reports.
f:sec-yield: A standardized fund yield the SEC requires: income over the last 30 days, minus expenses, as a yearly rate.
f:segment: A business line the company reports separately; revenue mix is each segment's share of total revenue.
f:sell-side: A researcher at a bank or broker who publishes earnings forecasts, ratings and price targets on companies.
f:shareholders-equity: A company's assets minus its liabilities on the balance sheet: the owners' share of the books.
f:sharpe-ratio: Return above a risk-free rate for each unit of volatility taken; higher means more reward per unit of swing.
f:short-interest: Shares sold short, a bet the price will fall, as a percentage of shares available to trade.
f:sp-500: An index of about 500 large US companies, weighted by market value and chosen by a committee.
f:spin-off: A company turns a division into a separate listed company and hands its shares to existing shareholders.
f:spot-crypto-etf: An exchange-traded fund that holds the cryptocurrency itself, so investors can own its price moves through a brokerage account.
f:stablecoin: A crypto token built to hold a steady value, usually one US dollar, typically backed by cash and Treasury bills.
f:stock-split: Dividing each share into several, lowering its price without changing the company's value; a reverse split combines shares.
f:straddle: A call and a put of the same expiry, at one strike (straddle) or two (strangle); buyers need big moves.
f:strike-price: The price at which an option's holder can buy (a call) or sell (a put).
f:tam: The total yearly spending on a product category: the most a company could sell with every customer.
f:tips: Treasury securities whose principal rises and falls with consumer prices; their yield is a real yield, the return above inflation.
f:total-return: The gain from the price change plus dividends, assuming each dividend is reinvested.
f:trailing-pe: The share price divided by the last 12 months' earnings per share: dollars paid per dollar of profit.
f:treasury-auction: How Treasury sells new debt: winning bidders all pay one price, set by the highest yield accepted.
f:treasury-bill: A US government loan of a year or less, sold below face value and repaid at face value.
f:treasury-note-bond: Loans to the US government that pay fixed interest every six months: notes run 2–10 years, bonds 20 or 30.
f:ttm: Trailing twelve months: the four most recently reported quarters added together.
f:vertical-spread: Buying one option and selling another of the same type and expiry at a different strike.
f:vix: Cboe's index of the volatility S&P 500 options are pricing over the next 30 days, as a yearly percentage.
f:volatility: How widely returns swing around their average, measured as the standard deviation and usually stated per year.
f:yield-spread: The 10-year Treasury yield minus the 2-year; a negative spread, an inverted curve, has often preceded US recessions.
f:yield-to-maturity: The yearly return from buying a bond at today's price and holding it to maturity, counting every coupon.
f:yoy: Year over year compares a period with the same one a year earlier; quarter over quarter, with the quarter before.
p:actions: The five things a player can do in turn: check, bet, call, raise or fold.
p:advantage-play: Methods that turn a game to a player edge by exploiting how it is run, such as card counting.
p:all-in: Betting every chip you have on the table, which no-limit games allow at any time.
p:angle-shoot: Using tricks that skirt the rules to mislead opponents, such as acting as if to fold.
p:ante: A forced bet posted before the deal, on top of the blinds; common in later tournament stages.

p:ante.tables: In casino carnival games, your main bet against the dealer, posted before the deal.

p:ante-bonus: Three Card Poker's extra Ante payout for a straight or better, paid whether or not you beat the dealer.
p:bad-beat: Losing a hand you were a strong favorite to win when an opponent catches a long-shot card.
p:banker-bet: The baccarat bet on the hand that draws last, paid even money less a 5% commission.
p:bankroll: Money set aside for gambling, apart from money needed for anything else.
p:basic-strategy: The mathematically best play for every player hand against every dealer upcard, given the table's rules.
p:bet: Put chips in first in a betting round; everyone after you must then call, raise or fold.
p:betting-system: A rule for changing bet size based on past results, such as doubling after every loss.
p:big-6-big-8: A bet that 6 (or 8) rolls before a 7, paid even money.
p:blackjack-side-bets: Optional bets on the first cards dealt, such as 21+3, Perfect Pairs and Lucky Ladies, each with its own paytable.
p:blackjack-switch: Blackjack played with two equal hands and the right to swap their second cards.
p:blinds: Forced bets posted before the deal by the two players left of the button, the small and big blinds.
p:bluff: A bet or raise with a weak hand that wins only if opponents fold.
p:bust: Going over 21, which loses at once.
p:button: A disc marking the dealer's position for the hand; it moves one seat left after every hand.
p:buy-bet: A place bet paid at true odds, less a 5% commission charged on the win or when it is placed.
p:call: Match the current bet to stay in the hand.
p:card-counting: Tracking dealt cards to know when the remaining shoe is rich in tens and aces, and betting more then.
p:carnival-game: A table game, often poker-flavored, played against the dealer with fixed rules and paytables.
p:cash-game: Poker played for the chips on the table, which stand for real money.
p:check: Pass without betting and keep your cards, allowed only while no one has bet in the round.
p:come-bet: Pass and don't pass bets made after the point is set, each with its own come-out on the next roll.
p:come-out-roll: The first roll of a new round of craps.
p:commission-free-baccarat: Baccarat with no 5% Banker commission; instead a winning Banker three-card 7 is a push.
p:community-cards: The face-up cards in the middle of the table that every player can use; five in hold'em.
p:comps: Rewards a casino gives players based on how much they bet: points, cash-back, meals, rooms.
p:continuation-bet: A flop bet by the player who made the last preflop raise, continuing to represent a strong hand.
p:cooler: A hand where two very strong hands meet and the loser couldn't reasonably have folded.
p:cost-per-hour: What a game costs in expectation for an hour of play: house edge × bet × decisions per hour.
p:das: Rule abbreviations: DAS allows doubling after a split; RSA lets a player re-split aces.
p:dealer-qualifies: The minimum dealer hand: a pair in Ultimate Texas Hold'em, queen-high in Three Card Poker.
p:degen: Short for degenerate gambler: someone who will bet on anything, at any odds, usually more than is wise.
p:deuces-wild: A video poker game in which every 2 is wild and stands for any card.
p:dice-control: The claim that a practiced grip and soft throw can make 7s rarer than 1 roll in 6.
p:dont-pass: The bet against the shooter, the reverse of pass except a come-out 12 pushes. House edge 1.36%.
p:double-down: Doubling your bet in exchange for exactly one more card.
p:double-exposure: Blackjack with both dealer cards dealt face up, paid for by the dealer winning most ties.
p:double-zero-wheel: A roulette wheel with 38 pockets, 1 to 36, 0 and 00, and a 5.26% edge on nearly every bet.
p:drawdown: The largest drop from a high point to a later low within a session.
p:edge-sorting: Reading tiny asymmetries in the printed backs of cards to tell high cards from low before betting.
p:element-of-risk: The house edge measured against all the money a player risks in a round, not just the first bet.
p:equity: Your average share of the pot: your chance to win if the remaining cards were dealt with no more betting.
p:even-money: Any 1-to-1 payout: a win pays the same amount as the bet.
p:expected-value: The average result of a decision if it could be repeated many times: each outcome times its probability, added up.
p:exploitative-play: Departing from balanced play to profit from one opponent's habits.
p:field: A one-roll bet: 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 11 and 12 win; 5, 6, 7 and 8 lose.
p:first-base: The first seat to the dealer's left, which acts first, and the last seat, which acts just before the dealer.
p:fish: A weak player who loses money over time, often without knowing it.
p:five-number-bet: A bet on 0, 00, 1, 2 and 3 on a double-zero wheel, paying 6 to 1.
p:fold: Give up the hand and any chips already in the pot.
p:fold-equity: The part of a bet's value that comes from the chance opponents fold.
p:free-bet-blackjack: Blackjack with house-funded free doubles on hard 9 to 11 and free splits, paid for by push 22.
p:free-odds: An extra bet behind a pass, don't pass, come or don't come bet, paid at true odds: no house edge.
p:full-pay: A machine with the best common version of its game's paytable; a short-pay machine has lines cut.
p:gamblers-fallacy: The belief that past independent results change the next one, such as red being due after a run of black.
p:grinder: A player who earns a modest, steady edge through long hours and volume.
p:gto: A strategy no opponent can profit against by changing their own play, approximated in practice by solver software.
p:hand-rankings: The order of five-card poker hands, royal flush down to high card: the rarer the hand, the higher it ranks.
p:hardways: A bet that 4, 6, 8 or 10 rolls as a pair before any other way or a 7.
p:heater: A winning streak better than skill alone would explain.
p:hit-frequency: The share of plays that return anything at all.
p:hit-stand: The two basic choices: hit takes another card, stand keeps your total and ends your turn.
p:hold: The share of money played that a machine keeps over time, the slot version of house edge.
p:hole-carding: Seeing a dealer's face-down card that a careless dealer exposes.
p:hole-cards: Your private, face-down cards: two in Texas hold'em.
p:house-edge: The share of each bet the casino keeps on average, built in by paying winners less than the true odds.
p:icm: A model that converts tournament chip stacks into shares of the prize pool.
p:implied-odds: Pot odds plus the money you expect to win on later streets if you hit.
p:index-plays: Departures from basic strategy at set true counts, such as standing on 16 against a 10.
p:inside-bets: Roulette bets on the numbered grid: a single number pays 35 to 1, a corner 8 to 1.
p:insurance: A side bet, offered when the dealer shows an ace, that the hidden card is a ten.
p:jacks-or-better: The base video poker game, where a pair of jacks or higher returns your bet.
p:kicker: A side card outside a hand's pair, two pair, trips or quads that still counts and breaks ties.
p:la-partage: Single-zero rules that return half, or hold over, an even-money bet when the ball lands on zero.
p:law-of-large-numbers: Over many independent bets, the average result per bet settles toward its expected value.
p:lay-bet: A bet that a 7 rolls before a chosen number, paid at true odds less 5% of the win.
p:losses-disguised-as-wins: A spin that pays back less than it cost but plays the winning sounds anyway.
p:max-coins: Betting the full five coins per hand, which raises the royal flush from 250 to 800 per coin.
p:mini-baccarat: Baccarat at a smaller table where the dealer handles every card, at 120–150 hands an hour.
p:natural: An ace and a ten-value card as your first two cards: a two-card 21.
p:near-miss: Two jackpot symbols on the payline and the third just off it.
p:nine-six: Shorthand for a Jacks or Better paytable: what it pays per coin for a full house and a flush.
p:nit: A very tight, cautious player who plays only premium hands and rarely bluffs.
p:nuts: The best possible hand given the cards on the board.
p:optimal-strategy: The play for every hand that maximizes long-run return under the game's rules and paytable.
p:outs: The unseen cards that would turn your hand into one that probably wins.
p:outside-bets: Roulette bets on groups of numbers: red or black, odd or even and high or low pay even money.
p:pair-plus: Three Card Poker's separate bet on your own three cards, ignoring the dealer.
p:pass-line: The bet with the shooter: wins on a come-out 7 or 11 or a made point. House edge 1.41%.
p:payline: A line across the slot reels on which matching symbols pay.
p:paytable: The printed schedule of what each result pays.
p:penetration: How far into the shoe the dealer deals before reshuffling, marked by a cut card.
p:place-bet: A bet that a chosen number rolls before a 7, with no come-out needed, paid at less than true odds.
p:player-bet: The baccarat bet on the hand that draws first, paid even money with no commission.
p:point: The number, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 or 10, set by the come-out roll.
p:position: Where you sit relative to the button, which sets the order of action. Acting later is an advantage.
p:pot-odds: The price the pot offers on a call: what you stand to win against what it costs.
p:progressive-jackpot: A jackpot that grows by a slice of every bet until someone hits it.
p:proposition-bets: Long-shot bets in the middle of the craps layout, mostly settled in one roll.
p:push: A tie between player and dealer: the bet is returned, neither won nor lost.
p:push-22: A rule where a dealer total of 22 ties every player hand still standing instead of busting.
p:q-6-4: The whole Three Card Poker strategy: play any hand of queen-six-four or better, fold anything worse.
p:raise: Increase the current bet, so the others must match the new amount to stay in.
p:rake: The card room's fee for running a poker game, taken from each pot, by the hour or from tournament entries.
p:range: The full set of hands an opponent could hold given their actions so far, instead of a single guess.
p:risk-of-ruin: The chance of losing an entire bankroll before reaching a goal or the end of play.
p:rng: The software that picks a slot's result the instant you press the button.
p:rounder: A player who makes a living from poker by making the rounds of games.
p:rtp: The share of money bet that a game pays back over the long run: 100% minus the house edge.
p:rule-of-2-and-4: A quick estimate of the chance to hit: outs × 4% with two cards to come, × 2% with one.
p:run-good: Results above or below expectation because of the cards, not the decisions.
p:s17-h17: Whether the dealer stands on a soft 17 (S17) or hits it (H17); the felt says which.
p:sample-size: How many hands, bets or sessions a result rests on.
p:semi-bluff: A bet with a draw: a hand that is probably behind now but has outs to become the best.
p:seven-out: A 7 rolled after a point is set; pass, come, place and buy bets lose, and the dice pass on.
p:shark: A strong player who wins by finding weaker ones and playing against them.
p:shoe: The box several decks are dealt from, typically six to eight in blackjack and eight in baccarat.
p:showdown: When two or more players remain after the last betting round, the hands are turned face up; the best wins.
p:side-bet: An optional extra wager beside the main bet, paid from its own paytable.
p:side-pot: A separate pot built from bets an all-in player can't match.
p:single-zero-wheel: A roulette wheel with 37 pockets, 1 to 36 plus one zero, and a 2.70% house edge on every bet.
p:soft-and-hard: A soft hand counts an ace as 11 and can't bust on the next card; every other hand is hard.
p:spanish-21: Blackjack with the four tens removed from each deck, face cards kept, offset by player-friendly rules and bonuses.
p:split: Turning a starting pair into two separate hands, each with its own bet equal to the first.
p:standard-deviation: Variance in money terms: the typical distance between a result and its expected value.
p:streets: The four betting rounds of hold'em: preflop, the flop (three board cards), the turn (fourth) and the river (fifth).
p:string-bet: Putting chips in with more than one forward motion without first announcing a raise.
p:super-fun-21: A blackjack variant, usually single deck, with many player gifts, paid for by naturals paying even money except in diamonds.
p:surrender: Giving up a hand after the first two cards and getting half the bet back.
p:tcp-ante-play: Three Card Poker's main game: post an Ante, see three cards, then fold or Play by adding an equal bet.
p:texas-holdem: Poker with two private cards per player and five shared face-up cards; the best five-card hand wins.
p:third-card-rule: Baccarat counts only a total's last digit, and a fixed table decides whether either hand draws a third card.
p:three-to-two: What a natural pays: at 3 to 2 a $10 bet wins $15; at 6 to 5 it wins $12.
p:tie-bet: The baccarat bet that Banker and Player finish level, usually paid 8 to 1.
p:tilt: Playing worse because emotion has taken over, usually after a bad beat or a losing run.
p:tournament: A fixed entry buys chips with no cash value; players who lose theirs are out, and top finishers are paid.
p:trips: Ultimate Texas Hold'em's optional side bet, paid on your own three of a kind or better, whatever the dealer holds.
p:true-count: The running count divided by decks left to deal, measuring how rich the remaining shoe is in tens and aces.
p:true-odds: The real chance of a result, as ways to lose against ways to win, versus what the casino actually pays.
p:upcard: The dealer's face-up card; the other, face down, is the hole card.
p:uth-ante-blind: Ultimate Texas Hold'em's two equal bets before the deal; the Blind pays a bonus only on a straight or better.
p:uth-play-bet: Ultimate Texas Hold'em's single raise: 4x or 3x the ante preflop, 2x after the flop, 1x after the river.
p:value-bet: A bet made to be called by worse hands, where a bluff hopes better hands fold.
p:variance: How widely results scatter around the expected value.
p:video-poker: Five-card draw on a machine: hold any of five cards, replace the rest once, get paid from a paytable.
p:vig: A fee taken out of a bet or its winnings, instead of being built into the payout.
p:volatility: How a game's payback is spread across its outcomes: small frequent wins, or rare large hits.
p:whale: A player who bets very large amounts, at poker or in the casino.
p:wheel-bias: A roulette wheel flaw, such as a loose fret, that makes some numbers come up more often than chance.
p:working: Whether a bet is live on a given roll; a bet that is off can't win or lose.
